newsitem.title: USA: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Dell still active post-split.
newsitem.headline: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Dell still active post-split.

text.p: Options on Dell Computer Corp were heavily traded in the stock's first post-split session, but traders said trading was not one-directional.
"We've got buyers and sellers," said Warren West, a market maker in the options at the Philadelphia Stock Exchange.
"The stock is extremely volatile, so premiums have expanded dramatically, which brings in a number of participants."
In late trade, Dell was down two at 79-1/2 on more than 15.2 million shares. The stock closed at 163 last Friday after dropping seven points.
The stock's decline Monday followed a downgrade by a Bear Stearns analyst who lowered his opinion to attractive from buy, citing the stock's lofty valuation.
Options traders have noticed a recent trend developing in which investors buy call options in a stock that is splitting.
Some of those investors were most likely selling out positions on Monday, traders said.

Among the Dell options, the August 85 call was most active, with turnover of about 6,930 contracts. The August 75 and 80 calls also were busy. Active puts included the August 80 and 85 and September 70.
Volatilities in the August and September Dell options was in the low- to mid-70 region, up from a historical volatility in the upper 40's.
West said the company's upcoming quarterly earnings report was also keeping premiums pumped up.
"With earnings you never know how good or how bad they're going to be so that increases premium and also increases speculation," he explained.
"So with a combination of events and the stock just being extremely volatile right now, it's pushing premiums up, which makes it much more attractive to a lot of people," he added.
West added that while most of the order flow was public paper, institutional activity was steady in the options.
Michael Schwartz, a managing director at Oppenheimer & Co, said Dell options volume has been high for a couple of weeks, rising in tandem with the rest of the PC group.
He added that the stock split, by automatically lowering options premiums, would likely keep the options busy over the near term.
In other activity, an investor apparently put on a collar in long term options on Philip Morris Cos Inc, Schwartz said.
The Philip Morris January 1999 40 put and January 1999 50 call each traded more than 3,000 contracts.
"It could be a collar where someone used proceeds from (selling) the out-of-the-money January 50 calls, to pay for the protection of the January 40 puts," Schwartz explained.
The January 1999 40 puts were trading at 4-1/2 in late trade and the January 50 calls were at 5-1/4.
The underlying stock was up 1/16 at 44-3/4.
The holder of the collar would be willing to sell the stock at 50 but would also have protection at 40 if the stock fell below that level.
